newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end a bit higher on short-covering.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end a bit higher on short-covering.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed modestly higher on Friday, buoyed by afternoon short-covering, and in the process ended the week with a more positive tone than where it began.

Late Friday, the 30-year bond was at 94-21/32, up 4/32 from Thursday, with its yield edging down to 7.06 percent from 7.07 percent. The bond's yield was at its lowest level on a closing basis since ending at 6.98 percent on March 26.
Treasury yields have fallen roughly a dozen basis points, recovering completely from heavy selling last Friday.
"The market has performed pretty well," said Brett Benza, senior trader at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp. "Some people are starting to turn more bullish."

Benza said the market was simply consolidating on Friday. "In this market, consolidation is good for the market," he said. "The market is in such a bear phase that any day you don't go down or do a little better has been a positive day."

Market activity was described as lackluster, as the market had little in the way of key economic data to trade on. Players concentrated on the expiration of May options, and tried to keep the current contract around the 108 level.
Treasury prices began the day slightly weaker, on light selling during overseas trading, which some said included foreign central bank sales of intermediates.

For the rest of the morning, Treasuries traded close to Thursday's closing levels. Dealers were seen creating short positions in hopes of padding the concessions expected ahead of next week's two- and five-year note auctions.

But, "the Street jumped the gun setting up for the auction," said a head trader at a primary dealership. Those shorts were squeezed, pushing Treasuries up nearly a quarter-point by mid-afternoon, the trader noted.
"It is tough to short a market on a thin, Friday afternoon," the trader added.

But the market's gains were partially erased as Federal Reserve Vicechair Alice Rivlin reiterated her concerns over inflation. She noted that worker insecurity, a decline in union power, and increased mobility of companies to operate in low-wage areas have kept wage-pressures from building.
"The real question is, how long will it last," Rivlin asked. "If unemployment stays low, will wage increases begin to accelerate and how much?"

Earlier in the morning, the market largely ignored a slight rise in the University of Michigan's consumer sentiment to 101.0 in mid-April from 100.0 in March. The current conditions index rose to 116.7 from 109.8, while the expectations index fell to 90.9 from 93.6.
Attention now turns to next week's upcoming auctions, in which players expect some concessions.
Traders said the market would love to take down the two-year note on Tuesday at 6.50 percent, but it is seen unlikely it will come in above 6.46 percent.
Late Friday, the when-issued two-year note was at 6.42 percent, while the when-issued five-year note was at 6.72 percent. Traders expect the latter to be sold at a yield above 6.75 percent.
Meanwhile, the two-year note was at 99-24/32, up 2/32, while its yield was down to 6.39 percent from 6.42 percent -- its lowest yield since April 7.
The five-year note was up 3/32 to 99-20/32 to yield 6.71 percent, and the 10-year note ended trade 3/32 higher at 95-28/32 to yield 6.83 percent.
Bill rates were down two basis points to up one basis point.
